svg.title: The signed-clock stall of the camp wait
svg.desc: The camp wait compares stamp + $14 with the sim clock word $2df72 as signed words, so a group camped before tick 32768 waits about 34,800 ticks once the clock passes 32768. Sources (reversing/powermonger/strategy.md): "Where it runs" (the $13000 listing: $1302e addq.l #1,$2df70), "The commander AI `$6522`" bullet "The signed-clock stall" (mechanism, W5G_k80 / W5G_k108 chunks: 1500 and 1843 decisions per chunk, 168 / 93 in the crossing chunk, 0 after; clock 32599 / 32674; stamps 2088 / 2038), "Isolation by clock pokes" (the five-row table, start L2G_k80_c8.snap, clock 11729, stamp 2088, stamp + 20 = 2108, about 167k steps per tick), "$51538 group-order table" (word 256 stamped by $3720). Literal scans of scratchpad/pm123/win/m1_map.ram $0..$40000: $2df72 in the instructions at $3720 and $65a0 only; the long $2df70 at $12f6 and $1352 (copies to $2df74), $1302e (increment), $1373c (compare with $2df74), $13baa (clr.l). LOAD note: strategy.md "The loaded camp stamps against the kept clock" and the stall bullet "A LOAD is a second way into the stall" (py/saveload/camp_stamps.py). Full fact list: clock_stall.facts.md.
svg.text: The signed-clock stall: the camp wait compares tick numbers as signed words
Box border = evidence. Green bars: the group decides ($65b4 reached); grey bars: it waits at $65a6.
proven
live (runs, with counts)
code read
inferred
PowerMonger (Bullfrog / Electronic Arts, 1990) is a war game in which the computer lords command armies through captains' groups. Their
commander AI ($6522) runs once per tick, the game's simulation step, and offers each group an order. A group that has just gone back to
camp is held for 20 ticks first: the game stores the tick at which it camped (its camp stamp) and waits while stamp + 20 is greater than
the current tick.
The bug: both numbers are 16-bit words and the compare is signed. Once the tick count passes 32768 the clock word reads as a negative
number, so every group stamped before then looks as if it camped in the future and waits about 34,800 more ticks, until the clock wraps
past 65536 and climbs back to its stamp. In a long game the computer's camped armies stop deciding. Panel A shows the code, B the
arithmetic, C the experiment that proves the cause, D the stall in untouched play.

g.text: as the group goes back to camp
the only reader: literal scan finds $2df72 twice

svg.text: How to read: the three instructions that touch the clock word $2df72. Left: the tick adds one to the long clock, whose low word is $2df72. Middle: a
group going back to camp copies that word into its record. Right: the wait test. bgt is the 68000's signed "branch if greater", so a clock word of
32768 or more is read as negative. A literal scan of the game finds $2df72 in these two instructions only.

g.text: B. One camped group, stamp 2088 (k80 group 0): clock in ticks since the land was built
At tick 34104 the word reads -31432 and 2108 > -31432, so the group waits. Groups that re-camp every few ticks (k143, k44: stamps within 20 ticks
of the clock) do not stall. Steps per tick differ per land, so the crossing falls at a different step count in each land.

svg.text: How to read: a number line of the clock in ticks since the land was built, with the signed value the compare sees underneath. The group camped at
tick 2088, so from tick 2108 it may decide (green). At 32768 the signed value jumps to -32768, 2108 is now "greater" than the clock, and the group
waits (grey) until the clock wraps and reaches 65536 + 2108.

g.text: C. Isolation by clock pokes: one write of $2df72, all from L2G_k80_c8.snap (clock 11729, about 167k steps per tick)
crosses 32768 at tick 16; last hit 2,346,222, then none
same write, no crossing in the budget: same as no poke
below 2108: waits about 60 ticks; first hit 9,711,010
waits until the clock reaches 2108: about 2140 ticks
Each prediction was written before its run; 5 of 5 met. With $7ff0, $6522 still runs (604 hits against 599), so only the compare at $65a0..$65a6 gates the decisions.

svg.text: How to read: one row per run. Every run starts from the same saved state, writes one value into the clock word and nothing else, and counts how often
the decision point $65b4 is reached (the first instruction after the compare). The bar is steps after the poke: green where decisions happen, grey
where the group waits. Steps are emulated 68000 instructions; M is a million, G a thousand million.
Takeaway: changing only the clock word switches the decisions off and on exactly where the signed compare predicts, and the AI routine itself keeps
running, so the compare is the cause.

g.text: D. Natural onset (W5G runs, py/arms/batch4.sh: 2G steps, then 20 chunks of 250M; $65b4 hits per chunk)
0 in chunks 12 to 20 (crossing chunk ends at clock 32674)
Bars are live counts; the pre-crossing rate is drawn flat from the one figure the doc gives. Chunk n covers 2G + (n-1) x 250M to 2G + n x 250M.

svg.text: How to read: two lands built with the game's Play Random Land option (the runs named k80 and k108) left to play with no input for 7G steps. Each bar
segment is one 250M-step chunk; the number is how often $65b4 was reached in it. The short segment is the chunk in which the clock passes 32768.
Takeaway: in untouched play the decisions stop within one chunk, at a different step count per land, because a tick costs a different number of steps
on each land.

g.text: Status: the compare is the cause in the emulator (proven by panel C). The same stall on a real ST or in Hatari is inferred from the code, not run.
Consequence: a natural run past 4.5G to 5.75G steps loses its idle camped groups' decisions for about the next 6G steps; zero late decisions do not mean an arm is unreachable.
Second route into the wait: a LOAD restores the saved camp stamps but keeps the destination's clock. lo.st into rand1 (clock 441), stamp 2088: first $65b4
predicted at clock 2108, about 279.2M steps; observed at clock 2108 after 276,745,802 steps (0.9% early). py/saveload/camp_stamps.py, proven by prediction.

svg.text: Terms and evidence
Proven: shown in the emulator by an experiment whose outcome was predicted before it ran (panel C, 5 of 5 predictions met; the LOAD route, one
prediction). Live: seen running in the emulator and counted. Code read: from the disassembly only. Inferred: a conclusion from the code that was not
run; here, that a real ST or the Hatari emulator stalls the same way, since the code is the game's own. A $ value is a RAM address in the game;
256(A1) is the camp stamp word of the group the AI loop is looking at. L2G_k80_c8.snap, rand1 and lo.st are saved states and a save file used as
starting points.
